                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

District Gilgit, capital of Gilgit-Baltistan, is strategically the most important territory in the Karakorum Range as it has been the trade center of the area for centuries. The historical Silk Route that promoted religious and cultural diversity to expand across borders adds to the significance of the district.

Languages: Shina is the local language while English and Urdu are widely spoken.

title: Swat
description: The lush green and historic Swat Valley, in the Malakand Division lies between 34o - 40' to 35o N latitude and 72' to 74o - 6’ E longitude and is part of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan. The valley is an integral part of the strategic and significant region where three parts of the Asian Continent—South Asia, Central Asia and China meet. The names found in ancient sources for Swat are Udyana and Suvastu because of the scenic beauty of the valley and the name of the river, respectively. The historical and cultural remains of the area provide evidence about human activities covering a large span of time. Alexander the Great came here in 327 BC en route India. In ancient times it remained center of Buddhism, still having its marks found from river bed to the tops of the mountains. During Abdul Wadud (1917- 1949) and Jahan Zeb's (1949-1969) peaceful region, Swati territories forming part of Swat State witnessed unprecedented development in the fields of education, health and communication. The magnificent Swat Valley popularly known as the Switzerland of the East, is situated north of Peshawar. In ancient times, it remained center of the then flourishing Buddhist civilization, still having its remnants found at various places. Its old name was Udyana (Land of Gardens). The archeological sites and monasteries dating back to Buddhist era add to its historical charm. Surrounded by majestic mountains, Swat Valley is full of roaring rivers, lush green forests and snow-covered peaks adding to its natural attraction. "Upper” and " Lower " Swat are terms in vogue based on the arbitrary demarcation of higher and lower regions In the valley by Swat River. Green fruit orchards, beautiful lakes, gushing streams and a fascinating landscape make it a place worth seeing.

title: Abbottabad
description:
It is charming spread out over several low, refreshingly
cool, and green hills. Abbottabad is 116 km (2 hours) from Rawalpindi and 208 km
(3 hours) from Peshawar. Abbottabad, which is 1,250 m approximately above sea level,
is a neat and clean town in a spacious valley surrounded by green hills. It is
a popular summer resort. It serves as a base for trips to Kaghan Valley and the
Gallies. KP-CTA maintains a Tourist Information Centre here to facilitate
visitors. Places worth visiting in and around Abbottabad are; Ilyasi Mosque
with a water spring, and the Shimla Hill viewpoint. Thandiani is another attractive
hill resort 30 km east of Abbottabad at an altitude of 2,800 meters above sea
level.

title: Swabi
description:
Swabi District Lies Between The Indus Rivers And Kabul Rivers. Swabi District Is Now Home To Many Excellent Educational Institutes But There Was No Public Sector University Till 2012. The Only Degree Awarding Institution Then Was Private Sector Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute Of Engineering Sciences And Technology, Which Was Inaugurated In 1993. In 2012, Government Of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Established First Public Sector University In Swabi, When It Upgraded Abdul Wali Khan University Mardan-Swabi Campus Into Full-Fledged University Of Swabi. While Women University Swabi Was Established In 2016, Swabi District Also Has A Public Sector Medical College Gajju Khan Medical College Swabi Which Was Established In 2014. Swabi District Is Currently Subdivided Into 4 Tehsils; Swabi Tehsil, Topi Tehsil, Lahor Tehsil And Razzar Tehsil.
 Swabi's historical significance is interwoven with its cultural fabric, evident in its archaeological sites like the ancient city of Raja Mehmoodabad. The district's strong Pashtun traditions infuse warmth, hospitality, and a sense of community. As a region advancing toward progress, Swabi has become an economic center driven by agriculture, commerce, and emerging industries. Its educational institutions contribute to intellectual growth, symbolizing the district's commitment to modernization.

title: Mardan
description: Mardan, District headquarter, the biggest town of Yousafzais and once the centre of Gandhara Civilisation, includes Takht-iBhai, Sahri Bahlol, Jamal Garhi, Shahbaz Garhi, Sikri, Chanaka Dheri and Palo Dheri as major Buddhist sites of Gandhara. A museum in Mardan has been recently opened. From Mardan, one can go to Shahbaz Garhi on Swabi road, where the Ashoka Rock Edicts are located. Many Buddhist legends are associated with this place, which is located at a distance of 15 km from Mardan. From here, the road goes further up to Asota Megaliths (’Stonehenge of Pakistan’) nearShiwa Adda on the Swabi Mardan road, and then to Swabi. At Swabi, the road bifurcates, one leading to Hund, the last capital of Gandhara under the Shahi rulers from the 7th-10th century AD. Mardan's historical significance is deeply ingrained, with ancient sites like the Takht-i-Bahi Buddhist monastery standing as testaments to its past. As the epicenter of Gandhara civilization, the district resonates with echoes of a rich history, while its Pashtun culture infuses warmth, hospitality, and a strong sense of community. Amidst this cultural legacy, Mardan has embraced progress, emerging as an economic hub driven by agriculture, commerce, and industries. The district's educational institutions contribute to intellectual growth, empowering future generations and paving the way for innovation and modernization.

title: Haripur
description:
Haripur District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, presents an intriguing blend of tradition and modernity. This district, characterized by its diverse population and cultural heritage, offers a captivating glimpse into the fusion of past and present. Festivals, crafts, and cuisine celebrate the vibrant cultural expressions that thrive amidst the backdrop of scenic landscapes, where rolling hills and fertile valleys create a serene ambiance.
 Economically vibrant, Haripur stands as a pivotal center of commerce, boasting a thriving industrial sector alongside its agrarian roots. Its educational landscape is equally impressive, with notable institutions nurturing intellectual growth and paving the way for progress. As the district strides forward, its commitment to sustainable development and enhanced social services positions Haripur as a promising destination for both cultural exploration and modern pursuits.

title: Mansehra
description: Mansehra District Is In The Hazara Division Of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province Of Pakistan. Mansehra District And Town Are Named After Man Singh, A Leading General Of Mughal Emperor Akbar. Mansehra Makes Its Boundary On The North To Kohistan And Battagram Districts, On The East To Muzaffarabad District Of Azad Jammu & Kashmir, On The South To Abbottabad And Haripur Districts And On The West To Shangla And Buner Districts. Mansehra District Is Dominated By High Mountains, The Famous Babusar Pass Is Situated On The North-Eastern Boundary Of The District. The Climate Is Cold In Much Winter And Pleasantly Warm In Summer. The Northern Part Like Kaghan Valley Is Cold In Summer And Extremely Cold In Winter And It Receives Heavy Snow Fall. The District Is Very Famous From The Tourism Point Of View And Has Been Blessed With Wonderful Scenery. Some Of Mansehra's Main Features Are Mountain Ranges, Plains, Valleys, And Numerous Lakes And Rivers. The Main Tourist Sites In The District Include Baffa, Dadar, Balakot, Kaghan Valley, Oghi, Shogran, Naran And The Famous Shrines Of Shah Ahmad Shaheed And Shah Ismail Shaheed, Who Fought The Battle With Sikhs In 19th Century, Are Also Historic Places To Visit. There Are Three Famous Lakes In The District: Lulusar Lake, Dudipatsar Lake And Saiful Muluk Lake.

title: Peshawar
description:
The Po-Lu-Shah of the Chinese, Pushapura of Persians and
Peshawar of the Mughal rulers the present capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
province of Pakistan was the second Capital of Gandhara under the Kushanas from
1-5th century AD it is the oldest surviving city in this part of Asia. Here,
once stood Asia’s biggest and most famous Stupa of Kanishka at Shahji ki Dheri,
outside the walled city’s Gunj Gate. The site was excavated in 1906-7 by D.B.
Spooner, the then curator of Peshawar Museum. The bronze relic casket
containing a crystal reliquary of Kanishka’s time was recovered from here. It
is now on display in the Peshawar Museum. The relics consisting of bones of
Buddha were gifted by the British rulers to the Buddhist Association of Burma
in 1910 and are now housed in the main pagoda in Mandalay. The Chinese
pilgrims, who visited Gandhara during 5th century AD, spoke of the glory and
richness of the Buddhist stupas and monasteries, especially the Kanishka stupa
and the famous Alms Bowl of Buddha displayed at one time in Peshawar. Gor
Khatri, Mahabbat Khan Mosque, Balahisar, Qissa Khawni Bazar, Mohallah Sethian,
Islamia College, Edwardes College, All Saints’ Church and St Jhon’s Cathedral,
Tomb of Nawab Syed Khan inside Mission Hospital, Durrani Graveyard, Governor’s
House and Peshawar Museum are some important features of Peshawar that merit a
visit.

title: Lower Dir
description:
Lower Dir District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, presents a captivating blend of natural beauty and historical significance. Its landscapes, adorned with rolling hills, fertile valleys, and meandering rivers, reflect nature's artistry, drawing nature enthusiasts to explore its scenic trails and discover the allure of the Hindu Kush mountains in the backdrop.
 Lower Dir's cultural heritage is deeply rooted in its rich history, with remnants of past civilizations interwoven into its tapestry. The district has witnessed the ebb and flow of various empires, from ancient times to more recent eras. As a historic crossroads, it has been influenced by the diverse cultures that traversed its lands along the ancient Silk Road. The legacy of these interactions can still be felt in the traditional practices, indigenous craftsmanship, and warm hospitality of its communities, offering visitors a genuine glimpse into its past.

title: Upper Dir
description:
Upper Dir is a picturesque district located in the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan. It is renowned for its stunning natural beauty, diverse landscapes, and rich cultural heritage. Situated in the northern part of the province, Upper Dir shares borders with Afghanistan to the west, the district of Lower Dir to the south, Swat district to the east, and Chitral district to the north.
 The district's landscape is characterized by lush green valleys, rolling hills, snow-capped mountains, and glistening rivers. It is a part of the larger Malakand Division and is known for its temperate climate, making it an attractive destination for both domestic and international tourists.
 Upper Dir is primarily inhabited by ethnic Pashtuns, and the Pashto language is widely spoken. The local culture is deeply rooted in Pashtun traditions, with traditional music, dances, and hospitality being integral parts of daily life.

title: Chitral Upper
description:
Under the shadows of Tirichmir in the Hindukush mountain
range, the valley of Chitral in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan is a
fascinating combination of scenic beauty and cultural diversity. The land of
majestic mountains, lakes, glaciers, and snow-covered peaks. Chitral stretches
from 1,094 m to 7778 m above sea level at Tirichmir Peak. With its collection
of rugged mountains, gushing rivers, hot springs, and fruit-laden orchards,
Chitral truly is an enchanting part of Pakistan. The area is bordered by
Afghanistan in the north and west, with the narrow Afghan Wakhan corridor
separating it from Tajikistan. Chitral can be accessed via several mountain
passes, the most famous being the Lowari Top (3,118 m) approximately crossing
the Hindu Raj (a spur of the higher Hindukush) in the south and the Shandur
Pass (3,798 m) forming the eastern gateway from Gilgit. Other passes include the
Dorah Pass from Badakhshan in Afghanistan and the Broghil (3,798 m) from the
Wakhan Corridor in Afghanistan. Although these two passes represented the main
arteries of the ancient Silk Route to Yarkand and Kashgar in China and
Badakhshan in Afghanistan, they are not much in use today

title: Charsadda
description: The ruins of Balahisar stand 29km to the northeast of Peshawar. One km north of the bridge at Jindi River, Charsadda.From here 5km down towards Takht-i-Bhai is Ghani Dheri Complex, the site of the Pushkalavati Museum. Thakht-i-Bhai town is located 20 km from Ghani Dheri and the Takht-i-Bhai Buddhist monastery is about 3km from the town. Identified by Alexander Cunningham as the first capital of Gandhara in the 19th century and excavated by Sir Mortimer Wheeler in 1958, it remained the first capital of Gandhara under the Achaemenids in the 6th century BC and was invaded by Alexander the Great in 327 BC

title: Malakand
description:
Malakand is a District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, offers a mesmerizing blend of natural splendor and historical significance. Its lush valleys, majestic hills, and winding rivers create a captivating backdrop that beckons exploration and awe-inspiring vistas. With a rich historical heritage, Malakand echoes with the whispers of ancient civilizations, bearing testament to its pivotal role as a historic crossroads. Archaeological treasures like Udegram stand as reminders of the district's connection to the Gandhara legacy, while its vibrant Pashtun culture imbues the region with a sense of community and warmth.
 Modern progress flows through Malakand's veins, as its economy thrives on the foundations of agriculture, trade, and emerging industries. Educational institutions, ranging from schools to colleges, play a vital role in shaping intellectual growth, exemplifying the district's commitment to both preserving its history and embracing contemporary development. Amidst its serene natural landscapes, Malakand invites visitors to embark on a journey that bridges the past and the present, immersing them in a district that is at once a custodian of its cultural heritage and a promising canvas for the future.

title: Karak
description:
Karak is a district of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province,
Pakistan. It is situated in the south of Kohat District and also share
boundaries with Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Mianwali and Warizistan districts on the
main Indus Highway (NA-55) between Peshawar and Karachi - it is 123 km from the
provincial capital Peshawar. History Until 1940, this whole area was ruled by
the Teri Nawab. Teri was the capital and the only Tehsil. It had tappas
(satrapies): Teri, Seni, Khurram and Barak. Between 1940 and 1982 it was a part
of Kohat, after the July 1, 1982, it has been a separate district. The district
is predominantly populated by Khattak tribe. The series of high and low
mountains of salt range enter into Karak from Punjab. There are large number of
salt mines in Jatta Ismail Khel, Garh jawal khel and Bahadar Khel areas. There
are also large number of mines of Gypsum in Jatta valley and Garh jawal khel.
District Karak is rich in Oil & Gas. The people of Karak are famous for
their hospitality.

title: Kolai Palas
description:
Kolai Palas, an alluring district in the embrace of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, unfolds as a realm of natural wonder and cultural mystique. This district's identity is intricately woven into its breathtaking landscapes, where towering peaks, verdant valleys, and dense forests converge to create a visual symphony of beauty. At its heart lies the Kolai Palas valley, a sanctuary of serenity, where time seems to slow down, allowing visitors to escape the bustling world and immerse themselves in nature's tranquility.
 Blessed with an abundance of biodiversity, Kolai Palas district serves as a haven for both flora and fauna. The district's diverse ecosystems provide a refuge for rare and elusive species, including the revered snow leopard and other remarkable wildlife. Amidst the natural grandeur, the local communities have preserved their cultural heritage, adding layers of human history to the district's tapestry. The warm hospitality and unique traditions of the inhabitants offer visitors an opportunity to glimpse into the soul of this enchanting land.

title: Shangla
description: A Very Beautiful District Next To Swat With Many Breathtaking Spots For Picnic And A Beautiful Scenery. A Lot Of Snow Fall Happens In Shangla In Winter. The Summer Season Is Normally Very Pleasant With Temperatures Ranging Between 15 To 25 Degrees In Most Places. The Main Places To Look Out For Are Shangla Top (Border Of Swat And Shangla, Yakhtange (Puran), Logay (Ajmir), Bilkanai, Ranyal Dam. Yakhtangay And Logay Are Very Popular Among Tourists For Picnics. Besham Is A Town Situated On The Bank Of Abasin (River Sindh) And Lies Half Way Between Islamabad And Gilgit On The Main Shahrahe Raisham Road Or More Popularly Known As The Silk Route In The World. Besham Is The Hottest Town In Shangla. Further From Besham Comes Dandai Which Is The Border Area Between Shangla And Battagram District. Most Of Shangla Is Covered In Mountains Including Some Very High Peaks.

title: Chitral Lower
description:
Lower Chitral had a sex ratio of 937 females per 1000
males and a literacy rate of 63.00% - 75.71% for males and 49.37% for females.
49,780 (17.89%) lived in urban areas. 27.10% of the population was under 10
years of age. 3,902 (1.40%) were from religious minorities, almost all of whom
are followers of the indigenous animistic Kalash faith that was once the
dominant faith in the district before the spread of Islam.
 89.48% of the population spoke languages recorded as 'Other'
on the census. Most of these spoke Khowar (or
Chitrali), the dominant language of Chitral as a whole. A minority spoke Chitral Kalasha and Wakhi ,
with the Kalasha dominating several valleys and the Wakhis spread
throughout the north of the district near the Afghan border. Pashto is
spoken in the southeast of the district by 9.11% of the population. There
are some speakers of the Madaklasht dialect , a Persian
dialect which is considered a mix of Dari and Tajik .
 Lower Chitral covers the area from lowari to Barenis and
Gobor in the Garam Chashma side.
 The unique culture of Chitral, developed over many millennia
with more than a dozen ethnic groups speaking as many languages, is closely
linked to that of Central Asia and China instead of South Asia, according to a
study conducted by International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
 It says that arts and crafts, traditional costumes, food and
beverages, local games, music, dance, folksongs and legendary sites form the
main components of the cultural heritage of Chitral. The study also includes
the historic military sites and indigenous tribes (Kalash) in the ingredients
of cultural heritage.
 “Chitral's artisans manufacture a wide range of elegant and
delicately crafted jewellery, woodwork and embroidery, woven and knitted
textiles,” the study says, adding that clay, wood, stone, bone, animal skin and
copper are the material most commonly used.
 The woolen fabric of Chitral, locally called shu, and
walnut-wood furniture are popular in handicraft markets throughout the country.
 The study adds that traditional clothes, including that of
Kalash people, are made from wool and silk and decorated with beads and shells.
 Traditional cap, (khapol) and gown (chugha) are popular
while the typical Chitrali shoes (khon) resemble the long riding boots.
 The area's vast culinary repertoire of foods and beverages
is unique in terms of both flavour and presentation.
 The study places music and dance at the heart of Chitrali
culture. Chitral's rich and varied musical tradition is part of the fabric of
everyday life while Chitrali sitar is famous throughout the world and the
traditional dances, such as dani and sauz are part of the folk heritage of
Central Asia.
 The folk poets of Chitral sing war songs as well as love
ballades, the study says, adding that epics are popular among the Kalash.
 “With its origin lost in the mists of antiquity, the ancient
tribe of Kalash is a unique cultural resource,” says the study, adding that
Chilm Jusht, Uchhal, Chitirmas are some of the main festivals of the tribe that
attract a large number of tourists to the three segregated valleys of Bumburate,
Birir and Rumbur in Chitral

title: Orakzai
description:
Orakzai emerges as a district of distinct character and historical significance. Set against a backdrop of rugged terrain and picturesque landscapes, this land holds stories that have weathered the test of time. Bordered by neighboring regions and embracing a rich tribal heritage, Orakzai encapsulates a blend of tradition and modernity.
 The district's landscape, a harmonious interplay of valleys and hills, tells tales of resilience and adaptation. Amidst these natural contours, the people of Orakzai have carved out their existence, maintaining cultural traditions while forging pathways toward progress. The region's tribal dynamics and historical evolution have woven a narrative that reflects the spirit of its inhabitants.
 As sunlight filters through the valleys and casts shadows on the ridges, Orakzai stands as a testament to the enduring spirit of its communities. It beckons those seeking to uncover its hidden treasures and engage with its hospitable residents, inviting a deeper understanding of the interplay between tradition and modernity in this captivating district.

title: Nowshera
description: Nowshera is a district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa near Peshawar, seamlessly marries tradition with progress. Its cultural tapestry, rich in Pashtun heritage, comes alive through vibrant festivals and traditional crafts that reflect the district's sense of community. Nowshera's strategic location fuels its economic vitality, with a thriving industrial landscape contributing to local employment and national economic growth. Amidst bustling markets and trade, Nowshera's educational institutions nurture intellectual growth, fostering a generation of thinkers and professionals. The district's natural beauty, including the scenic River Kabul, offers a serene escape, complementing its efforts toward sustainable development and improved civic amenities. In Nowshera, the past and present harmoniously converge, inviting travelers and enthusiasts to explore its dynamic blend of culture, commerce, and natural charm.

title: Dera Ismail Khan
description:
This is one of the biggest and most important cities of the Southern
region of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Situated on the Western bank of the Indus River, the
old city used to be surrounded by a mud wall having ten gates. Some of the gates
are know as Imaman Wala, Topanwala, Thatharanwala and Powindah Seraiwala. The city
is a trading center and famous for wood and embroidery works. The city was
founded by Malik Suhail Baloch in the 15th century AD and he named it after one of
his son.

title: Battagram
description: The District Battagram Is Surrounded By Kohistan District To The North, Mansehra District To The East, Kala Dhaka Tribal Area To The South And Shangla District To The West. Its Headquarter Is At Battagram Town At A Distance Of About 75 Km From Mansehra On The Silk Highway. The District Consists Of Two Tehsils, Battagram And Allai. It Has A Number Of Beautiful Valleys And The District Covers An Area Of 350,172 Acres. The District Is Mostly Mountainous With Peaks Rising Above 4000 Meters With Thick Forests. However, Fertile Plain Areas Exist In Nindhyar, Tijri Deshan, Batamori, Banna And Rashang Valleys. Plenty Of Springs And Streams Flow Through Out The District, Providing Water For Drinking And Irrigation. There Are Two Main Streams (Locally Called Khawar) I.E. The Nindhyar Khawar And Allai Khawar. Nindhyar Khawar Originates In The Mountains Of “Hill” And After Flowing Through The Main Village Joins Indus River At Thakot In The East. The Other Big Stream, The Allai Khawar Originates In Chaur Mountains And Joins The Indus River At Kund In The East. The Climate In Battagram Is Moderate In Summer And Severe Cold In Winter. Upper Parts Of The District Especially Shamlai, Hill And Bilandkot Of Battagram Tehsil And Sorgai, Rashand, Gangwal, Bateela And Pashto Batangi Of Allai Tehsil Receive Heavy Snowfall. Chaur Is Snowbound And Inaccessible For Eight Months In The Year.

title: Kohat
description:
Kohat was founded by Raja Kohat in the 4th century BC. It
saw many ups and downs in history. The Sikh built a fort here, which was
modified by the British and stands magnificently in the heart of the town. On
one side of the fort are the famous Jangal Khel springs, with banyan trees
around. Just outside the fort are a boulder, well and vhill-gah (meditation
place) associated with Hazrat Syed Abdullah Haji Bahadar Kohati (RA). He lived
in the times of Aurangzeb Alamgir and his shrine is located inside the city.
There is also a grand mosque near the shrine. The shrine of another Holy man
Hazrat Bona Pir (RA) is situated north of Kohat at the foot of the hills
and is visible from miles away. There is also a perennial spring near the
shrine.

title: Kohistan
description:
Kohistan District, situated within the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, is a district of captivating contrasts that encapsulates both rugged natural beauty and a rich cultural heritage. The district's diverse topography encompasses majestic mountains, fertile valleys, and meandering rivers, creating a picturesque landscape that beckons nature enthusiasts and adventurers. Kohistan's geographical composition lends itself to outdoor exploration, offering hiking trails, stunning vistas, and a serene environment that resonates with both locals and visitors.
 Steeped in history, Kohistan holds echoes of ancient civilizations and trade routes, shaping its cultural tapestry. The district's communities are infused with traditions, customs, and craftsmanship that bear the marks of its historical interactions. The warmth of its people and their genuine hospitality reflect a sense of unity and shared identity. As Kohistan embraces progress, it strives to maintain its unique character, fostering a balance between preserving its cultural roots and embracing modern developments. In essence, Kohistan is an invitation to delve into a land where nature's splendor and historical legacy converge, creating a destination that offers a glimpse into the heart of a captivating district within Pakistan.

title: Lakki Marwat
description:
The town of Lakki was founded as Ihsanpur by Fateh Khan Tiwana in 1844.
The town was shi ft ed to its present
location in 1864. It derives its present name from Diwan Lakki Mal of the
Sikhs. It is an important trading center and headquarter of District Lakki
Marwat. The population comprises mainly of Marwats and also includes Mina Khel,
Khoidad Khel and Syed Khel.

title: Buner
description:
Buner District, cradled within the embrace of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is a captivating realm where history, nature, and culture converge harmoniously. Its picturesque landscape, adorned with rolling hills, lush valleys, and meandering rivers, creates an enchanting tableau that beckons both locals and visitors alike. Rich in heritage, Buner reveals its ancient secrets through landmarks like the Takht Bhai Buddhist monastery, a testament to its historical significance along the ancient Silk Road. This district is a canvas painted with the vibrant hues of Pashtun traditions, where intricate embroidery, traditional attire, and spirited folk music flourish, fostering a strong sense of community and warmth among its residents.
 Buner's heartbeat resonates with agrarian rhythms, as terraced fields yield bountiful crops like wheat, maize, and fruits, sustaining the livelihoods of its inhabitants. As Buner embraces modernity while cherishing its roots, it holds promise for sustainable growth and responsible tourism. The district's allure lies not only in its breathtaking landscapes and historical treasures but also in its commitment to preserving its cultural heritage and natural splendor, ensuring that Buner remains a captivating destination that bridges the past with the aspirations of the future.

title: Bannu
description:
Bannu is and old town west of the Tochi Vally. The old town
was surrounded by a high mud wall, having gates in all directions. The Sikhs
built a fort here, which was named as Dilip Garh or Dilip Nagar after Maharajah
Dilip Singh. This is the biggest Sikh fort in the frontier, with mud walls and
bastions. The British had named the town as Edwards Abad and a British Cemetery
exists in the Cantonment are. The Airport known as Islam Bibi Airport was named
after the Hindu girl, who converted to Islam in the mid-1930s. The ancient site
of Akra is located in the district.

title: Hangu
description:
Hangu District, situated at the heart of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, offers a captivating blend of historical significance and tranquil landscapes. Its diverse terrain, characterized by rolling hills and fertile plains, creates a picturesque backdrop that beckons exploration and contemplation. Hangu's rich Pashtun traditions contribute to a sense of warmth and community, making it a destination that embraces both its history and the promise of modern development.
 Hangu's commitment to progress is reflected in its higher educational institutions, which play a pivotal role in nurturing intellectual growth. These institutes contribute to the district's intellectual landscape, empowering a generation of thinkers and professionals. As Hangu strides forward, its economy thrives through agriculture, commerce, and emerging small-scale industries. Amidst its serene natural beauty, Hangu stands as an inviting haven, where visitors can immerse themselves in a district that harmonizes the echoes of its past with the aspirations of a vibrant future, while education remains a cornerstone of its evolving identity.

title: Tank
description:
The town of Tank is about 65 kilometers away
from Dera Ismail Khan. This big trading center has a large ruined mud fort
constructed by Sarwar Khan in the early 19th century AD. Sir Henry Durand, the
lieutenant Governor of the then Punjab Province was killed here in 1870 while
sitting on an elephant and trying to pass through one of the gateways.

title: Torghar
description:
Torghar is a district located within the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan. Nestled amidst the picturesque landscapes of the country, Tor Ghar is renowned for its breathtaking natural beauty and its significance in the local cultural and historical context.
 The Tor Ghar region is characterized by its towering peaks, deep valleys, and diverse ecosystems. Its name "Tor Ghar" translates to "Black Mountain," which aptly describes the dark, rocky terrain that dominates the landscape. The mountains are known for their strategic location and have played a role in the region's history, with ancient forts and remnants serving as a testament to their historical importance.
 Despite its challenging topography, Tor Ghar is inhabited by resilient communities that have thrived amidst the harsh conditions. The people of Tor Ghar have a unique way of life, deeply rooted in tradition, and their cultural practices have stood the test of time.

title: Khyber
description:
District Khyber, nestled within the Peshawar Division of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province in Pakistan, stands as a testament to the region's evolving administrative landscape. Formerly designated as an agency within the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), this district experienced a significant transformation in 2018. With the momentous merger of FATA into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, District Khyber emerged as an integral and distinct entity within the provincial framework.
 This transition marked a historic shift in governance, elevating Khyber from its previous agency status to a formal district structure. This evolution unlocked new avenues for development, local governance, and representation, aligning the district with the dynamic political and administrative landscape of Pakistan.
 Encompassing a diverse geographical expanse, District Khyber stretches from the captivating Tirah valley to the bustling city of Peshawar. This range of landscapes reflects the district's unique blend of natural beauty, cultural heritage, and strategic significance. Khyber's journey embodies the nation's commitment to unity and cohesion, exemplifying a broader vision of inclusive governance and regional integration.

title: Kurram
description: Kurram District, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, In the northeastern reaches lies the Afghan province of Nangarhar, featuring iconic landmarks such as the renowned Tora Bora and the majestic Koh-E-Safed. Koh-E-Safed's lofty mountain ranges, annually adorned with a snow-white blanket, emerge as a natural geographical boundary between Afghanistan and Pakistan, their towering presence shaping a distinct border. To the west, the Afghan province of Paktia extends its embrace, intricately weaving connections with Kurram District, while to the south, the district of Khost completes this interplay of proximity. Meanwhile, the eastern edge of Kurram converges harmoniously with Tull in Pakistan's Hangu District, forming a dynamic nexus of cross-border interactions and cultural entwinement. In Kurram, mountains and narratives converge, forging a compelling tale of geographical divisions and human connections.

title: Mohmand
description:
Mohmand District, encompassing an area of 2296 square kilometers, is home to a population of approximately 466,944. This district, while relatively compact in size, holds significant importance. Agriculture and minerals stand as its prominent sectors, shaping the local economy and livelihoods. Despite its potential, the cultivated area accounts for only about 9% of the total land, reflecting the challenges of limited arable land.
 Water scarcity poses a significant concern across various parts of the district, underscoring the need for sustainable water management strategies. Amidst these challenges, agriculture remains a vital contributor, with vegetables taking center stage among its predominant products. These crops not only sustain local communities but also serve as a source of trade and commerce.

title: South Waziristan
description:
South Waziristan is a district in Dera Ismail Khan division
in the rugged heart of Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, South Waziristan
stands as a region of captivating contrasts and historical significance.
Bordered by neighboring districts and Afghanistan, this land bears witness to a
rich tapestry of cultures and histories. The region's undulating landscapes,
characterized by arid plains, lush valleys, and jagged peaks, tell stories of
resilience and adaptability.
 South Waziristan's history is deeply intertwined with its
tribal heritage, where traditions have thrived for generations. The region's
complex social fabric has witnessed shifts and transformations, playing host to
diverse communities that have shaped its identity. The towering Shawal and Spin
Ghar mountain ranges from natural barriers, revealing the district's unique
topography and offering a vivid portrayal of the challenges and opportunities
that define life here.

title: North Waziristan
description:
The North Waziristan borders in the
north with Kurram and Kohat, in the east with Kohat and Bannu, in the south
with the South Waziristan and in the west with Afghanistan. The district is the
second largest in previous FATA, with an area of 4,707 square kilometers.
 The district presents huge potential
in mining sector as huge reserves of copper has been identified while Chromite,
Manganese reserves are also available. Furthermore, oil and gas reserves are
also being explored by KPOGCL and it is expected to add towards growth of North
Waziristan in near future. Miran Exploration Block is located in North
Waziristan and Kurram agency. Investment opportunities for local and foreign
companies in E&P are available via joint venture.
 South and North Waziristan are both
highest producers of pine nuts (Chalghoza) and Pakistan is reported to be the
second highest exporter of pine nuts after China. However, due to lack of
training in harvesting, cutting, roasting and processing there is high
percentage of wastage. Value addition in pine nut handling is strongly
recommended.

title: Bajaur
description:
District Bajaur, situated within the Malakand Division of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province in Pakistan, holds a distinctive position in the region's administrative landscape. Previously designated as an agency of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), this district underwent a significant transformation in 2018. With the historic merger of FATA into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Bajaur emerged as a distinct and integral district within the province.
This transition marked a pivotal moment in Bajaur's governance, as it shifted from its previous administrative framework to the formal structure of a district. This change brought about new opportunities for development, local governance, and representation, aligning the region with the evolving political and administrative landscape of Pakistan.
Bajaur's history and geography contribute to its unique character, as it continues to navigate the path of progress within the larger framework of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The district's journey exemplifies the nation's commitment to unity and integration, reflecting a broader vision of inclusive governance and regional cohesion.

title: Astore Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

Astore District is one of the ten districts in Gilgit−Baltistan, with its administrative centers located in Eidgah and Gorikot. To the north, it borders Gilgit District, while Roundu District lies to the northeast, and Skardu District to the east. To the southeast is Kharmang District, and to the west is Diamer District. The district also shares its southwestern boundary with Neelum District of Azad Jammu and Kashmir and its southern border with Bandipore District in the disputed Kashmir region administered by India.

Languages: Shina is the local language while Urdu and English are also used for communication across the valley.

Popular activities: The lakes in the area are famous for fishing and angling.

Famous Tourist Spots: Rama Valley is densely forested with huge pine, cedar and juniper trees. Rama Lake of the valley is one of the most stunning attractions

title: Skardu Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

District Skardu in Baltistan Division is located at the confluence of Indus River and Shayok River that leads toward the legendary tourist destination of the greatest mountain peaks of the world. Skardu Valley is path to some of the highest mountain peaks in the world such as Gasherbrum, K2, and K3. This region is the manifestation of hospitality and respect for tourists.

Languages: The native tongue of people of Skardu is Balti, however, English and Urdu are widely spoken.

Famous Tourist Spots: Some of attractive tourism destinations of Skardu are Kharpocho Fort, Manthal Rock (Buddha Rock), Sadpara and Kachura Lakes, and the wonderful Shangrila lake. The beautiful valleys of Chunda, Basho, Bilamik & Satpara are also worth a visit. This region also hosts the golden desert of Katpana Sand Dunes (the cold desert) and milky water streams of Hargisa.

Popular Activi

title: Diamer Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

District Diamer is gateway to Gilgit-Baltistan. The area manifests prehistoric traces of human species and advancement in the shape of rock carvings, rock inscriptions and petroglyphs etc. These features make Diamer district an important destination with over 35000 prehistoric inscriptions and carvings. The biggest power generation project of the country, the Diamer-Bhasha Dam adds to the economic importance of the region.

Languages: Local language is Shina, however, English and Urdu are also widely spoken.

Famous Tourist Spots: The important valleys of Diamer district include Tangir, Darel, Chilas (hub of archeological sites in the area), Bunar Das, Gonar Farm and Raikot. The beautiful Fairy Meadows is the most pleasing destination for national and international tourists.

Popular activities: The famous and captivating Nanga Parbat (8125m) that cheers trekkers

title: Shigar Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

Shigar district is gateway to great Karakoram, covers an area of 8,500 sq. km. It is located on an ancient trading route from Central Asia. At the head of the Braldo Valley is Baltoro Glacier, 35 miles long, and Shigar's own northern ridge rises to a height of 28,265 ft, the pinnacle of which is the K2, the world's second highest peak. Shigar valley is nearly at half an hour drive from Skardu. It has a vast agricultural land and several attractive tourist spots. The fertile land of Shigar is irrigated with Shigar River. It is abundant in fruits like grapes, peaches, pears, walnuts and apricots. The valley stretches to 170 km from Skardu to Askole. Famous Tourist Spots: The restoration and conservation of heritage sites in Shigar is praiseworthy. The 400 years old Shigar fort, which has been restored and is being used as a heritage museum, is a great example of reu

title: Ghanche Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

Ghanche is easternmost district of Gilgit-Baltistan. It is home to a wide range of historical sites and architectural points of interest including Chaqchan Mosque and Khaplu Palace - both exemplify local craftsmanship and traditional woodwork. Kashmiri craftsmen brought over by the rulers of Khaplu incorporated both local and Kashmiri building elements to develop a range of splendid structures in the region. Ghanche district has its own cultural festivities and the people of the district love to celebrate the festivities occasionally with their traditional tunes, dance and songs. The famous dances of the region are Mandoq Taimo and Ragi Taimo.

Languages: Balti is the local language while Urdu and English are also spoken.

Famous Tourist Spots: Khaplu palace, a prime example of Royal residence in the area, and Chaqchan Mosque; the oldest mosque in Baltistan.

Popu

title: Ghizer Tourist Destinations
description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

District Ghizer is westernmost part of Gilgit-Baltistan, which borders Wakhan strip to its north-west, the Chitral District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa towards its west, the Diamer District to its south, and the Gilgit District lining its eastern edge. The highest peak in Ghizer is the Koyo Zom (6,871 m), a part of the Hindu Kush Range that acts as a boundary between Ghizer and Chitral. Some notable mountain passes in this district are the Shandur Pass, the Qurumbar Pass, the Hayal Pass, the Bichhar Pass, the Thoi Pass, and the Darkot Pass. The Koh-i-Ghizer, Golaghmuli, Ishkoman and Yasin valleys are a few of the most historically significant valleys in the district.

Languages: Shina, Khowar, Brushashki and Wakhi are common languages while Urdu and English are also widely spoken.

Formerly a princely state, the district of Hunza covers an area of 11, 695 sq km. It is home to a wide range of cultural heritage sites including the famous Altit and Baltit Forts, historic polo grounds, watchtowers, mosques, and several archaeological sites such as the renowned Sacred Haldekish Rocks in Ganish. Hunza Valley is the prime attraction for tourists as it offers spectacular sceneries of mountains. Tourists can witness high peaks of 7000m such as Lady Finger and Ultar. Hunza has been bestowed with natural beauty rich cultural and traditional heritage such as traditional dresses, tunes, dances and cuisines. It is famous for its delicious apples, apricots, mulberry, cherries and grapes.

Languages: Burushaski, Shina and Wakhi are local languages while English and Urdu are also widely spoken.

It has countless hidden and open treasures of precious gems such as Ruby, Topaz, Aquamarine, Emerald and Quartz among several others. description:
GOVERNMENT OF GILGIT BALTISTAN 
                                Tourism, Sports, Culture, Archaeology & Museums Department

The name Kharmang belongs to Balti language which is comprised of two words, Khar means "Fort" and Mang means "abundant". So, Kharmang means the valley of Forts. The name was given to the valley during the era of Ali Sher Khan Anchan who built many forts in the area because of its geographical importance. The old name of this valley was Khartikhsha.

Previously Kharmang was part of Skardu district, however, it became a separate district in 2015. It is located about 120 kilometers from Skardu city while Tolti serves as the district headquarters.

The valley is known for its enchanting waterfalls, lush fields, meadows, high mountains, and fresh fruit, particularly its renowned apples, apricots, and cherries, due to its unique geography and climate.
